title: Threat Model Spec — First-Party PDLC Self-Assessment (Dogfood Run 1)
description: First-party threat model analysis of the threat-model-spec project itself, produced via tms analyze across the product-definition, builder-definition, and implementation PDLC stages (INIT-THREATMODELSPEC-002, RMI-THREATMODELSPEC-113). The system under review is the tms analyze analysis pipeline: the mechanism by which AI agents read PDLC-stage artifacts, produce structured claims, and merge them into a canonical ThreatModel document.

authors.name: product-definition-analyst, builder-definition-analyst, implementation-analyst (tms analyze dogfood run 1)

diagrams.title: tms analyze Pipeline
diagrams.description: How PDLC-stage artifacts become canonical ThreatModel content: an agent reasons over resolved inputs and returns structured claims, which tms validates and merges atomically.

elements.label: PDLC-Stage Artifacts
elements.description: Specs, source code, IaC, telemetry — resolved as Artifact objects in plan mode. May be first-party, third-party, or open-source; not always fully trusted.

elements.label: tms analyze
elements.description: Orchestrates: resolves inputs, opens an AnalysisRun, and atomically validates+merges an agent's AnalysisResults. Performs no analytical reasoning itself.

elements.label: Stage Analyst Agent
elements.description: Reads the resolved artifacts and PDLC-stage report profile, reasons about them, and writes an AnalysisResults JSON file. The reasoning step happens entirely outside tms.

elements.label: Canonical ThreatModel Document
elements.description: The merged, validated model — read by humans and by later-stage agents as trusted input.

flows.label: 2. hand agent resolved artifacts + report profile
5. read by a later-stage agent as trusted context

threatActors.name: Adversarial content author (compromised dependency, malicious PR, or attacker-controlled analyzed system)
threatActors.description: An actor who cannot directly compromise tms itself, but can influence the content of an artifact that a stage-analyst agent will read (e.g. a compromised third-party repo under the third-party profile, or a malicious pull request to a first-party repo under CI).
primaryGoals: Suppress or misdirect a real finding by manipulating what an analysis agent reads or what its output claims
Embed instructions in analyzed content that a downstream AI agent might follow when it later reads the merged model

mitigations.title: Document that agent/artifact-sourced free-text fields are untrusted data, not instructions, at every point they're read
mitigations.description: Add an explicit warning to tms analyze's own help text and to every stage-analyst agent spec's process, stating that Evidence.Excerpt, Finding.Title/Description, and ArchitectureAssertion.Observed originate from analyzed content or another agent's output and must never be interpreted as instructions by whoever reads them next (human or agent) — matches sr-agent-content-not-instructions from the product-definition stage.

assets.name: User-authored ThreatModel documents
assets.description: ThreatModel JSON files end users create to describe their own systems' architecture, assets, threats, and mitigations.
assets.value: Reveals a user's own attack surface, unpatched risk, and control gaps if disclosed to an adversary targeting that user's system.

assets.name: tms analyze trust chain (Artifact -> AnalysisResults -> canonical ThreatModel)
assets.description: The sequence by which artifact content and agent-authored claims become part of the canonical, trusted ThreatModel document that humans and later-stage agents rely on.
assets.value: If this chain can be manipulated, the canonical threat model itself becomes an unreliable security record — the core value proposition of the product.

scenarios.title: Prompt injection via merged analysis-result content
preconditions: Attacker controls or influences content that will be resolved as an Artifact for a stage analysis (e.g. a third-party repo's README, or a first-party repo's PR diff analyzed in CI)
A stage-analyst agent reads that content, and its raw reasoning output becomes an AnalysisResults file merged into the canonical model without independent verification of the claims themselves
attackPath: Attacker embeds adversarial instructions in analyzed artifact content (e.g. a code comment, README section, or commit message worded to look like a directive to an AI reader)
A stage-analyst agent, reasoning over that artifact, is influenced by the embedded instructions and produces AnalysisResults reflecting the attacker's intent rather than an honest assessment
tms analyze --apply merges the result: schema and referential-integrity validation pass (the JSON is well-formed), but nothing checks the semantic honesty of the claims
A later PDLC-stage agent, or a human reviewer, reads the merged model's free-text fields as trusted context and is itself misled or manipulated
scenarios.outcome: A real vulnerability could be recorded as resolved/false-positive, or a fabricated finding could waste review time — either way, the canonical threat model's authority as a security record is undermined without any schema-visible sign of tampering.
scenarios.businessImpact: Erodes the core value proposition of the product (PRD Goal 1: 'one JSON-based ThreatModel type is the source of truth') if the source of truth can be steered by adversarial input with no structural guardrail against it.

locator.section: UC5: Agent-Assisted Threat Modeling with LLM-as-Judge Evaluation

evidence.excerpt: An AI agent produces or extends a threat model from an architecture description; a judge pipeline ... grades the result ... before a human reviews it.
evidence.summary: PRD commits the product to AI agents reading and writing ThreatModel documents as a primary use case, not an edge case.

evidence.excerpt: FR10: LLM-as-Judge evaluation integration ... FR13: Agentic AI threat modeling fields: agent capabilities, execution context, credential flow tracking
evidence.summary: The product explicitly models AI-agent execution and credential-flow risk elsewhere in its own domain vocabulary, but has no stated invariant governing trust in content that agents themselves author into the canonical document.

evidence.excerpt: Threat Model Spec does not implement SAST, DAST ... It is the data format those activities' inputs and outputs are represented in — a scanner or agent produces findings; Threat Model Spec is where those findings live, referenceable and mappable.
evidence.summary: By design, tms is a durable record for analysis output produced by other tools/agents — which makes the trustworthiness of that stored output a first-party product concern, not something tms can defer to 'the scanner's problem.'

locator.section: 4. Agent Workflows ... The tms analyze command

evidence.excerpt: (4) hand the agent the workflow spec and gathered inputs — the agent reasons and returns findings/evidence/claims as the output-object contract; (5) validate and write them into the model under the run
evidence.summary: The TRD's own architecture description confirms step 5 validates structure (schema, referential integrity) but does not describe any check on the semantic honesty of what the agent claims in step 4 — the trust boundary crossed here is architectural, not a bug.

evidence.excerpt:
AI coding agent (Claude Code) ── runs ──▶ tms analyze --stage --profile

(does the reasoning) (loads profile + inputs, drives workflow, writes the run, grades it — no reasoning)
evidence.summary: tms is explicitly scoped to never reason about content — by design, it cannot itself distinguish an honest agent claim from a manipulated one. Any such check has to live either in the agent or in a later human/judge review step.

evidence.summary: Every AnalysisResults object is appended into the canonical model verbatim. No field is sanitized, truncated, or tagged as originating from analyzed content — the only gate before the write is candidate.Validate() at line 260, which checks structure and referential integrity, not content.

AnalysisResults and the types it carries (Finding.Description, Evidence.Excerpt, ArchitectureAssertion.Observed, etc.) use plain Go string fields with no wrapper type, struct tag, or doc comment marking them as untrusted/agent-sourced content requiring careful handling by a reader.

securityRequirements.statement: Free-text fields populated from analyzed artifacts or agent-authored AnalysisResults (Evidence.Excerpt, Finding.Title/Description, ArchitectureAssertion.Observed) must never be treated as executable instructions by a human reviewer or by a downstream AI agent reading the merged ThreatModel — they are data describing what was found, not directives to follow.

A ThreatModel document merged via tms analyze --apply must pass full referential-integrity validation before any bytes are written to disk — no partially-invalid document is ever persisted as canonical.

architectureAssertions.expected: An invalid merge (dangling references, malformed structure) must never be partially or fully persisted to the canonical model file.
architectureAssertions.observed: Confirmed during this very dogfood run: an earlier apply attempt with a SecurityRequirement.originArtifactId pointing at an Evidence ID instead of an Artifact ID was rejected outright, and the model file was left byte-for-byte unchanged (cmd/tms/analyze.go runApplyMode builds a candidate copy and calls candidate.Validate() before any write).

architectureAssertions.expected: Per builder-definition's mitigation-provenance-warning-on-agent-content, tms analyze's help text and every stage-analyst agent spec should warn that merged free-text content is untrusted data, not instructions.
architectureAssertions.observed: As of this analysis run, no such warning exists in cmd/tms/analyze.go's Long help text or in any agents/specs/agents/*.md file.

findings.title: Agent-authored AnalysisResults cross a trust boundary into the canonical model with no semantic verification, only structural validation
findings.description: The boundary from 'artifact content + an agent's own untrusted reasoning' to 'canonical ThreatModel content read as ground truth by humans and later-stage agents' is crossed by tms analyze --apply with only schema and referential-integrity checks (TRD step 5). This is a real, design-level trust boundary per the product-definition stage's scenario-prompt-injection-via-merged-analysis finding, now localized to the exact architectural seam that crosses it.

findings.title: AnalysisResults free-text fields carry no structural or documented signal that their content is untrusted
findings.description: This confirms at the implementation level what the builder-definition stage flagged at the design level (finding-untrusted-merge-boundary): runApplyMode's merge loop (cmd/tms/analyze.go:247-254) appends every AnalysisResults field into the canonical model with zero sanitization, truncation, or provenance-warning attached to the content itself. The only gate is candidate.Validate() at line 260, which is purely structural (schema shape + referential integrity — see ir/validate.go), not a content check. AnalysisResults' own type definition (ir/analysis_results.go) uses bare Go strings with no doc-comment or wrapper signaling 'this text originated from analyzed material, treat as data not instruction.' Reachable: any tms analyze --apply invocation feeds this path, including one driven by an agent reading attacker-influenced artifact content under any profile (first-party CI on an external PR, third-party, or open-source).
